primitives.name: Rank Product Scoring
primitives.verbatim_quote: Under this "triathlon" format, every climber must compete in all three concentrations, and their individual score is determined as the product of the ranks across the three disciplines, with the lowest rank product declared the winner.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'R_i': 'rank in discipline i (dimensionless)', 'S': 'total score = R_1 × R_2 × R_3 (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Each discipline contributes independently to total score; ranks are ordinal and bounded.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When one discipline rank approaches infinity, S → ∞; when all ranks equal 1, S = 1.

layer2.mapping: Rank product encodes competitive dominance across disciplines; GSI infers climber strength; GSE simulates state evolution through ranked transitions.
layer2.telemetry: Observed rank-product distribution vs. simulated expectations

primitives.name: Discipline Bias Analysis
primitives.verbatim_quote: Finally, this work finds evidence that the current competition format is putting speed climbers at a disadvantage.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'B_s': 'bias factor for speed climbers (dimensionless)', 'P_s': 'probability of medal for speed climber (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Performance in speed does not linearly correlate with bouldering or lead performance.
primitives.breakdown_regime: B_s < 1 implies systematic disadvantage; P_s decreases with increasing B_s.

layer2.mapping: Bias manifests as non-uniform rank-product variance; GSI detects deviation from uniformity; GSE models skill transfer between domains.
layer2.telemetry: Climber rank-product variance by discipline type

primitives.name: Olympic Medal Distribution
primitives.verbatim_quote: However, since only one set of Olympic medals is awarded to each gender event of sport climbing at Tokyo 2020, all three disciplines were included together, forming one single combined event.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'M_k': 'medal rank k ∈ {gold, silver, bronze} (dimensionless)', 'S_k': 'score threshold for M_k (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Medal allocation is based on rank-product thresholds; scores are independent of external factors.
primitives.breakdown_regime: S_k increases monotonically with k; S_gold < S_silver < S_bronze.

layer2.mapping: Medal thresholds define outcome partitions; GSI computes posterior probabilities of medal placement; GSE simulates progression paths to podium.
layer2.telemetry: Score thresholds for gold/silver/bronze vs. actual medal winners

The rank-product scoring system operates as a multiplicative ordinal kernel across three distinct performance domains—speed, bouldering, and lead climbing. Each climber’s score S = R₁ × R₂ × R₃ encapsulates their relative standing in each discipline. This formulation introduces a geometric mean-like structure where a single poor performance in one domain can disproportionately penalize overall competitiveness. The system assumes independence among disciplines, yet empirical data suggests that speed climbers face inherent disadvantages due to differing skill sets required for each discipline. The resulting score distribution exhibits skewness favoring those who excel consistently across all domains. In the context of Olympic competition, where only one medal set per gender is awarded, this scoring mechanism creates a dual challenge: it incentivizes balanced performance while simultaneously introducing systemic bias toward climbers specializing in multiple disciplines. The derived kernel enables probabilistic modeling of advancement likelihood and medal chances, allowing GSI to compute posterior distributions over climber rankings and GSE to simulate optimal performance trajectories through multi-event transitions.
